attributes.title: Greenfield vs Brownfield: Resource Import & Code Generation
attributes.description: Learn how to import pre-existing cloud infrastructure into Terraform state using legacy CLI imports and modern declarative import blocks with automated HCL code generation.

post.html:
Greenfield vs Brownfield: Resource Import & Code Generation

By the end of this lesson

Adopt an existing object without unintended changes.

Not all infrastructure starts from a blank slate (Greenfield). Most DevOps engineers inherit pre-existing, manually created cloud infrastructure (Brownfield) that must be brought under Terraform management without downtime.

1. The Two Approaches to Importing Infrastructure

2. The Modern Declarative import Block (Terraform 1.5+)

In Terraform 1.5.0 and newer, importing is declarative and supports automatic code generation.

Step 1: Declare the import Block

Create a file named imports.tf:

# imports.tf

import {
  to = aws_vpc.imported_vpc
  id = "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890" # Existing AWS VPC ID
}

import {
  to = aws_security_group.imported_sg
  id = "sg-0987654321fedcba0"  # Existing AWS Security Group ID
}

Step 2: Generate HCL Code Automatically

Run terraform plan with the -generate-config-out flag:

terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated_resources.tf

Terraform queries AWS APIs for vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 and writes a starting resource configuration to generated_resources.tf:

# generated_resources.tf (Generated by Terraform)

resource "aws_vpc" "imported_vpc" {
  cidr_block           = "172.31.0.0/16"
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  enable_dns_support   = true
  instance_tenancy     = "default"

  tags = {
    Name = "legacy-production-vpc"
  }
}

Step 3: Review and Apply

Initialize a root module with the AWS provider and the correct account/region first. The output path must not already exist when generating configuration. Review generated defaults, conflicting arguments, secrets, and resource ownership; import does not recursively adopt attached resources.

After correcting the generated file, review a new plan. Proceed only when the intended result is import-only:

terraform apply
# Output:
# Apply complete! Resources: 2 imported, 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

3. The Legacy Imperative Method (terraform import)

For reference or older environments:

  1. Write the resource block in main.tf:
    resource "aws_s3_bucket" "legacy_bucket" {
  # Leave empty or add bucket name
  bucket = "my-pre-existing-company-bucket"
}
  2. Run the import command:
    terraform import aws_s3_bucket.legacy_bucket my-pre-existing-company-bucket
  3. Run terraform plan and adjust arguments until Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

Apply the idea: review an import-only plan

A successful import binds an existing ID to one Terraform address. It does not establish that generated defaults match your operational requirements. If the import plan also replaces or updates the object, stop and reconcile the configuration. Avoid binding one remote object to two addresses or states.

Check your understanding: Will importing a VPC automatically import its subnets and routes?

No. Determine which related objects and provider resource types need separate declarations/imports, and assign clear ownership for each.

Read further: Official documentation.

4. Summary & Next Steps

Declarative import blocks streamline brownfield migrations and eliminate manual guesswork. Next, in Section 04: Multi-Environment SDLC Architecture, we will explore how to isolate Dev, Staging, and Production environments safely.
